name: GHK-Cu
summary: A small copper-binding peptide found naturally in human blood, used in skin creams and injected for skin, hair and healing, based mostly on small cosmetic and animal studies.
what_it_is: GHK-Cu is the tripeptide GHK (glycine, histidine and lysine) bound to copper. GHK occurs naturally in human plasma, saliva and urine, and its plasma level falls with age. In laboratory and animal research it increases collagen and elastin production and speeds wound repair. It is used in cosmetic skin products and is not an FDA-approved drug.

evidence.why: Skin benefits come from small cosmetic studies of copper-peptide creams in women, mostly presented at meetings by researchers tied to the developer; healing benefits come from animal studies, and FDA says human data on injections are limited.

status_us.label: Non-injectable compounding allowed; injectable under review
status_us.note: FDA lists GHK-Cu for non-injectable use in Category 1 (under evaluation), which its interim policy lets licensed pharmacies compound under set conditions. Injectable GHK-Cu came off the Category 2 safety-risk list in April 2026 after its nomination was withdrawn, which did not make it eligible for compounding; FDA's advisers are expected to review it before the end of February 2027, with no date set.

benefits.claim: Fewer fine lines, shallower wrinkles and thicker, denser skin with copper-peptide face and eye creams over 12 weeks in small studies of 41 to 71 women; most were presented at meetings rather than peer-reviewed
More collagen production in women using a copper-peptide thigh cream for one month than with vitamin C or retinoic acid creams, in a small pilot study
Faster skin recovery after irritation or tape stripping in human test models, using copper-peptide mixtures rather than GHK-Cu alone
Faster wound healing with more new blood vessels and collagen in rabbits, rats, mice, pigs and dogs, including diabetic wounds in rats
Raises collagen and elastin production and acts on many genes and pathways, according to reviews of mostly laboratory research

risks.risk: Possible immune reactions to injected GHK-Cu, because the peptide can clump and carry peptide-related impurities, according to FDA
Limited human safety data, especially for injections; reviews calling it very safe come from researchers linked to its developer and give no formal safety data

avoid_if: Wilson disease or another copper-handling disorder (it carries copper; ask a clinician first)

before: General health check with a clinician
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for GHK-Cu by any route.

studies.title: GHK Peptide as a Natural Modulator of Multiple Cellular Pathways in Skin Regeneration
studies.people: Summary of small cosmetic studies in 41 to 71 women each, human skin-irritation models and animal studies
studies.finding: Copper-peptide creams improved wrinkles, skin density and thickness over 12 weeks, and GHK-Cu sped wound healing in several animal species. The authors, from the developer's company, call it very safe but report no formal safety data.

studies.title: Regenerative and Protective Actions of the GHK-Cu Peptide in the Light of the New Gene Data
studies.finding: GHK increases collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycan production and improves tissue repair; gene data suggest it acts on many biochemical pathways at once.

ask_your_clinician: Is there a proven treatment for my skin, hair or healing goal that I should try first?
Is a topical product enough, and what are the risks of injecting a peptide that FDA says may cause immune reactions?
Could the copper in it matter for any condition I have?

notes_for_editor: Status nuance: FDA's May 14, 2026 503A list says non-injectable GHK-Cu was removed from Category 1 on April 22, 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn, then re-added after a May 5, 2026 clarification; injectable GHK-Cu sits in the 'nominated but withdrawn' table on FDA's Category 2 page. Both are slated for advisory committee consultation before the end of February 2027 (sources 2, 4, 5). An HHS 'Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides' went to the White House on October 14, 2026 and was unpublished as of October 16 (source 5); re-check before publishing. The human skin studies (Abdulghani 1998; Leyden 2002; Finkley 2005) were read only as summarized in a developer-affiliated review (source 6); the originals are meeting presentations, a university report or a book chapter. No human studies of injected GHK-Cu were found. Hair-growth claims were not supported by the sources opened and are left out. The Wilson disease caution is an inference from its copper content. Source 7 was read as an abstract only (PMC full text blocked by a bot check). WADA's 2026 list does not name GHK.
